summary: The quality requirements for replacement Yom Kippur goats: when a replacement is needed, the finest available goat should be chosen, and the replacement pair must be matched with each other just like the original pair. The quality standard doesn't relax in contingency scenarios. This reflects the principle of hidur mitzvah (beautifying the commandment) as applied to the Temple service - in Israel's relationship with God, the best is always owed.

learning.ahaMoment: Even in replacement scenarios, the Yom Kippur standard demands the best. The circumstances may be difficult but the quality requirement is unchanged - the relationship with God is not compromised by operational challenges.
learning.memoryAnchor: Even in replacement: the best available is owed to God. The standard doesn't drop because the situation is difficult.
learning.learnerQuestion: When replacing a disqualified Yom Kippur goat, is any valid matching animal sufficient, or must the replacement be of equal or superior quality to the original?
learning.coreTension: In contingency scenarios, quality standards might reasonably relax since the ideal pair is no longer available; yet the Mishnah insists on choosing the superior replacement even in an already-disrupted situation.
learning.coreMove: The principle of hidur mitzvah (beautifying the commandment) applies to contingency scenarios without relaxation; the obligation to offer the best available animal is unconditional - the disruption does not lower the quality standard, and the replacement pair must still be matched in appearance, height, and value.

takeaway.text: When a Yom Kippur goat requires replacement, the superior available animal must be chosen; hidur mitzvah and matching requirements apply to replacement pairs with full force, reflecting that quality obligations for Temple service are unconditional rather than situational.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume contingency scenarios allow quality relaxation since the ideal has already been disrupted; they miss that hidur mitzvah is not conditional on circumstances and applies with full force even when the original ideal conditions have been lost.

rashiTranslations.en: 'It shall stand in its place' - he designates a substitute only for the one that died, but for the surviving one
he does not designate a substitute to disqualify it and have this new one take its place. 'As it stands, so it stands' - meaning it remains in its own sanctity,
and we do not say it becomes rejected. 'I do not know which "second"' etc. - this refers back to the Mishnah: the 'second' that we taught
shall graze - I do not know which, etc. This is how we read it: 'and not the one whose partner died' - meaning, not this one
whose partner died. 'It shall stand alive, and not that it already
stood' - and then became rejected through its partner's death,
and now comes to stand again: it shall stand
alive with a single standing, not two standings.
'The one to be sent away shall die' - this shows that living animals
can become rejected. 'When I said it follows the Rabbis, I meant according to the Rabbis' view' -
for since Rabbi Yehuda says 'and furthermore,' to teach us
that living animals can become rejected, this implies he has heard
the Rabbis say that the second of the first pair is offered,
since living animals are not rejected, and the second of the
second pair shall graze, since a communal sin-offering does not die;
and he comes to disagree with them on two points: as for what
you say, that a communal sin-offering does not die, I
say it does die; and furthermore, not regarding the one you said
shall graze do I say it shall die, but rather
it shall be offered, and instead the second of the first pair shall die.
'This works out well according to Rav: this is what Rabbi Yehuda
and the Rabbis dispute' - regarding this "and furthermore" of the latter clause. 'But
according to Rabbi Yochanan' - who says that even the Rabbis said that the second of
the first pair shall graze, on what point does
Rabbi Yehuda disagree with them in this latter clause that states
'and furthermore'? 'This works out well according to Rabbi Yochanan' - who says
that the Mishnah's ruling of 'it shall graze' is stated regarding the second of the first pair;
you find that in the corresponding individual case,
it would die, on account of the principle of a sin-offering whose owner has
achieved atonement. 'In accordance with Rabbi Abba' - who said, in tractate
Temurah (23a), regarding the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis about one who set aside his sin-offering
and it was lost, and set aside another in its place, and then the first was found, so both now stand:
Rabbi says atonement is achieved through one of them and the other must die, while the Sages say a sin-offering
whose owner achieved atonement dies only when found after the owner already achieved atonement, but
if found before atonement and after the setting-aside, it grazes. And Rabbi Abba said regarding this: all
agree that if atonement was achieved through the one not lost, meaning the second one set aside last,
the lost one dies, for so was it stated as a law given to Moses at Sinai: a sin-offering that was lost,
and its owner achieved atonement through another, the first one dies; they disagree only where atonement was achieved through the first one
and the second remains standing. And this is the point of their dispute: Rabbi holds that one set aside to replace a lost animal
is treated like a lost animal, while the Rabbis hold it is not. And regarding our Mishnah here: this works out well
according to Rabbi Yochanan, who says the Mishnah's 'it shall graze' refers to the second of the first pair - this is why it gives
the reason that a communal sin-offering does not die, whereas an individual's in this case would die, since it would be
a case of atonement achieved through the one not lost while the rejected one still survives, and all agree that one dies.
'But' - the comment is completed on 65a as 'according to Rav,' continuing the challenge of how Rav's own view can explain this same Mishnah clause.
